message.content: Without using any tools, write 700 words about the DEC VT320 and VT420, in plain paragraphs with no headings and no lists.

content.text:
By 1987 the video terminal was a mature product in a shrinking market, and the VT320 reflects that clearly. It was DEC's cheapest serious terminal to date — a small, monochrome, text-only unit that did nothing flashy and did it reliably. Customers who wanted ReGIS or Sixel graphics bought its siblings, the monochrome VT330 or the colour VT340; everyone else, which meant most VMS and Ultrix sites filling rooms with green-screen workstations, bought the VT320 by the crateload. It was in many respects a VT220 refined rather than replaced: the same fundamental control vocabulary, the same twenty-four by eighty default, but faster, smaller, and considerably less expensive to put on a desk.

What the VT320 did add was mostly a matter of capacity and correctness. It answered `DECSCL` at conformance level 3, one step above the VT220, and it supported ISO 8859-1 alongside DEC's own Multinational Character Set — a quiet but consequential concession that the wider industry, not DEC, would decide how accented characters were encoded. It carried multiple pages of screen memory, so a host could compose a form on an off-screen page and flip to it instantly rather than repainting line by line, and it offered several page lengths beyond the traditional twenty-four lines. The LK201 keyboard carried over, later joined by the LK401 with its additional modifier and Compose keys.

The VT420 of 1990 is the more interesting machine technically, because it is where DEC added features that modern terminal emulators are still catching up with. The headline addition was rectangular area operations: a family of sequences that treat a bounded box of cells as a single object. `DECCRA` copies a rectangle from one part of the screen to another, `DECFRA` fills one with a given character, `DECERA` and `DECSERA` erase one, and `DECCARA` and `DECRARA` change or invert video attributes across one without touching the characters underneath. On a 9600-baud serial line these were enormously valuable — scrolling a sub-window or highlighting a block became a handful of bytes instead of a full repaint — and they anticipate, in hardware, exactly the operations a windowing text application performs constantly.

Alongside them came horizontal margins. The VT100 had given applications a top and bottom scrolling margin through `DECSTBM`, which is why fixed headers and status bars are trivial to implement; the VT420 completed the picture with `DECSLRM`, left and right margins enabled through the `DECLRMM` mode. With both sets of margins in force, a program could define a genuine rectangular sub-window that scrolled independently of everything around it — side-by-side panes, each moving on its own, without the host redrawing a single unaffected cell. It is a striking capability to find in a 1990 serial terminal, and it went largely unused for decades because by the time anyone cared, people were writing for emulators that had not implemented it.

The VT420 also supported two concurrent host sessions multiplexed over a single physical line, presented as a horizontally split screen, and it retained and extended the page memory scheme so applications could move between stored pages directly. A PCTerm mode let it emit PC scan codes for software that expected them — an accommodation that says a great deal about where the market had gone. The VT510 followed in 1993, and shortly afterwards DEC sold the terminals business outright; it passed to Boundless Technologies, and the line wound down as PCs running emulation software made dedicated hardware unnecessary.

The afterlife is where these two machines still matter. Terminfo carries `vt320` and `vt420` entries, but far more significantly, xterm implemented the VT420's rectangular operations and left-right margins, and other emulators followed unevenly — some support `DECSLRM`, some ignore it, and applications consequently probe rather than assume. The result is that a feature designed to save bytes on a serial cable now exists as an optional fast path in software running on machines a hundred thousand times faster than a VT420, occasionally exercised by a text editor doing a split-pane scroll. The VT320 sold better and is remembered less; the VT420 sold into a dying market and left the deeper mark on the protocol everyone still speaks.
